precepts.text: Correction is grievous unto him that forsaketh the way: and he that hateth reproof shall die.
precepts.point: But if ye turn away, and forsake my statutes: definition read in class, forsake means to abandon, desert, or leave entirely, a breach of duty. Then will I pluck them up by the roots, and make them to be a proverb and a byword among all nations. Reading that is understanding why we went into captivity.

note.label: Listen, Learn & Live The Art of Enduring in The Truth

precepts.why:
The Lord warned Solomon, “if ye turn away, and forsake my statutes and my commandments”; to forsake means to abandon, desert or leave something entirely, a breach of duty, to totally turn your back. Proverbs ties forsaking to hating correction: “Correction is grievous unto him that forsaketh the way: and he that hateth reproof shall die.”

When you have forsaken the way, being corrected is grievous to you. You keep having to be told the same thing over and over, and the one who doesn't want to hear it gets pissed off; he doesn't want to hear it no more. That was Solomon, the old and foolish king who would no more be admonished.

And the end of it is death: “he that hateth reproof shall die.” For Israel it meant being plucked up by the roots out of the land and made a proverb and a byword among all nations. Reading that is understanding why we are in captivity today. We got jammed up because we would not take correction.

precepts.text: A reproof entereth more into a wise man than an hundred stripes into a fool. A foolish person cannot allow wisdom to enter in; you sit around the men, you are in the school with all these men, you see everybody growing around you, but the wisdom cannot take hold because you are fighting against it.
precepts.point: That is why some have been here 10 or 15 years and are still a soldier or an officer of 10. You cannot say you have been held back: you know everything else, but the wisdom cannot take hold and exalt you like it exalts the rest that take hold of it. That is when it is time to take stock in yourself, and a lot of people do not want to do that.

note.label: Character & Integrity: The Hidden Strength Behind Wisdom

precepts.why:
“He that refuseth instruction despiseth his own soul”. He doesn't want to hear it; he doesn't want to be corrected; he's always right, but wrong as hell. That isn't hurting somebody else; you are destroying your own soul, because you can't be corrected, which means you can't grow. This is why: “A reproof entereth more into a wise man than an hundred stripes into a fool.”

As a foolish person, you cannot allow wisdom to enter in. You're sitting around the men, you're in the school with all these men, you see everybody growing around you, and for some reason you know everything, but the wisdom can't take hold and exalt you the way it exalts all the rest who take hold of it. You're fighting against it.

That is why some have been in the truth 10 or 15 years and are still a soldier. How long you been with us? 10 years. What's your rank? Officer of 10, sir. Why? I don't know, sir. You know. You know everything else but that. You can't say you've been held back. Ten years and you're only able to deal with ten men: that is a problem.

That is when it is time to take stock in yourself, and a lot of people don't want to do that, because they don't want the integrity that comes with the Bible. The one who hears reproof gets understanding; the fool takes a hundred stripes and learns nothing.

precepts.text: Correction is grievous unto him that forsaketh the way: Cain forsook the way over a process of time, and the correction became grievous. And he that hateth reproof shall die, because the wages of sin is death.
precepts.point: And Cain talked with Abel his brother: this is the deception. He acted like his friend, talked with him over a period of time, and lured him out to the field. And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him. That is the spirit you are rolling in when you move with that bitter spirit; in that wrath you will slay a brother, or in that bitterness you might betray a brother.

note.label: Bitterness: The Hidden Leaven From Cain To Esau

precepts.why:
Cain was born first, just like Esau. “Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground”, a man of the field, which already tells you what is going on. “And in process of time it came to pass, that Cain brought of the fruit of the ground an offering unto the Lord.” Cain already knew right from wrong, because his father taught him animal sacrifice, but over a process of time Cain turned evil and did not do what the Lord commanded.

Abel brought “of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof. And the Lord had respect unto Abel and to his offering:” “But unto Cain and to his offering he had not respect. And Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell.” His countenance fell because he was corrected. What really started all of this? Correction.

Solomon says, “Correction is grievous unto him that forsaketh the way”. Cain had forsaken the way over a process of time, so the correction was grievous to him. That grievous spirit nourished bitterness, and the bitterness grew until he murdered his brother. That is the spirit you are rolling in when you move with a bitter spirit.

Then: “and he that hateth reproof shall die”, because the wages of sin is death. Paul says, “For if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged.” If we judged ourselves we would not have to be told about the bitterness, envy, hatred and malice inside us; when we refuse, the Lord has to bring the chastening. Cain refused to get himself right, and he became the father of wickedness.

precepts.text: I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding. Your pastors could have been the covetous men of the world; the Lord led you to pastors who help you build. So why stay away from them, or go on the quest to have fun rather than to learn?
precepts.point: A fool looks for who he can talk sports or his job with; a man seeking knowledge seeks the war room. Some brothers think they already have the wisdom and do not need leadership, and then correction comes and they move like a woman, all emotion.
precepts.why:
“The heart of him that hath understanding seeketh knowledge.” Where is that knowledge going to come from? From the leadership. Jeremiah shows it: “And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding.”

Your pastors could have been the negroes in the world, leaders who just seek after covetousness. But the Lord led you to pastors according to his heart, brothers who are able to help you build and help you see yourself. They feed you with knowledge and understanding, so that is who you seek after.

So why do you keep running away from them? On the quests there are brothers who show up just to have fun. You see them once, turn around, and they are gone for days: they were not on the quest, they were on a cruise. They are not going for any wisdom, knowledge or understanding whatsoever.

That is the fool of Proverbs 15, whose mouth “feedeth on foolishness”: when leadership is in the room, he looks for who he can talk sports or his job with. The man who has understanding seeks the war room and seeks the water from the Bishop, the Deacons, the captains and the officers. That is what leadership is there for, and this whole Bible is about knowledge, wisdom and understanding that we have to seek out.

precepts.text: The eyes of the Lord are in every place, beholding the evil and the good.
precepts.point: The Lord gives a dispensation of time and grace to get the mind right, to repent, pray, and fast over what we struggle with; the just man falleth seven times and riseth up again. When leadership corrects you, do not think evil of them: the Lord did not have to send leadership, he could have sent evil your way instead; correction is the warning and the mercy.

note.label: Joshua 7: The Accursed Thing and the Sin of Achan

precepts.why:
Joshua said to Achan, “hide it not from me”, because it was already not hidden from One mightier than he: we cannot hide what we do from the Lord. “The eyes of the Lord are in every place, beholding the evil and the good.” He sees everything we do.

If you are in this walk as a manpleaser, the Lord sees what you do away from the brotherhood and the sisterhood. Achan hid what he took from men, but not from the eyes that are in every place.

precepts.text: The eyes of the Most High are in every place, beholding the evil and the good, so there is no hiding from him.
precepts.point: Though Job were righteous, yet would he not answer, but would make supplication to his judge.

note.label: Job 9: No Man Can Contend With God

precepts.why:
“Lo, he goeth by me, and I see him not: he passeth on also, but I perceive him not.” Job cannot see him, but he is there: “The eyes of the Lord are in every place, beholding the evil and the good.”

There is nothing we can do to escape him; his omnipresence and omnipotence reach wherever we go. We can run but we cannot hide. And when he taketh away, who can hinder him? No man can say to God, Lord what are you doing, I do not agree, I veto that, I object your honor. If he will not withdraw his anger, the proud helpers stoop under him, so how much less can Job choose out his words to reason with him. Though he were righteous, he would not answer, but make supplication to his judge.

precepts.text: The eyes of the Lord are in every place, beholding the evil and the good.
precepts.point: Thick clouds are a covering to him that he seeth not, and he walketh in the circuit of heaven. Eliphaz says God is surrounded by thick clouds and cannot judge through them, but that is when God is really looking, when you think he is not.

note.label: Job 22: Acquaint Now Thyself With Him

precepts.why: “The eyes of the Lord are in every place, beholding the evil and the good.” Eliphaz asks, “How doth God know? can he judge through the dark cloud?”, and says thick clouds are a covering to him that he seeth not. But the eyes of the Lord are in every place. There is no dark cloud he cannot judge through; he beholds the evil and the good. That is when God is really looking, when you think he is not.

precepts.text: The eyes of the Lord are in every place, beholding the evil and the good, so even when you think nobody is watching, he sees.
precepts.point: Job says his righteousness he holds fast and will not let it go, and his heart shall not reproach him so long as he lives, saying he is not a hypocrite; what he says, he does.

note.label: Job 27: I Will Not Remove My Integrity From Me

precepts.why:
Job says, “till I die I will not remove mine integrity from me.” Integrity is the quality of being honest and having strong moral principles: moral uprightness, honesty, good character, righteousness, doing what is right even when no one is looking.

Someone is always looking: “The eyes of the Lord are in every place, beholding the evil and the good.” Even when you think nobody is watching, he sees. Job kept the commandments to the best of his ability because he loves the Lord and fears the Lord; he did what he was supposed to do when nobody was watching, not just getting in order when the righteous come around or when he feared correction from men.

It is like the ring of Gyges in Plato's Republic, a ring that turns you invisible. The question of ethics is whether you still do the right thing and uphold your integrity, or go against everything you learned in uprightness. You do good whether you are invisible or not, faithful to the Most High and keeping his laws at all times, because his eyes are in every place.

precepts.text: A merry heart makes a cheerful countenance, but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken.
precepts.point: The health of the countenance ties to a merry heart. You can always tell when someone carries something heavy; a broken spirit shows on the face. If you truly pay attention to somebody, you can tell when things are not going well with them.

note.label: Psalm 43: Send Out Thy Light and Thy Truth

precepts.why:
“hope in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God.” The health of the countenance ties to a merry heart: “A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken.”

You can always tell when someone carries something heavy; a broken spirit shows on the face. If you truly pay attention to somebody, you can tell when things are not going well with them. That is why the psalmist questions his own soul, asking why it is cast down and disquieted, and answers himself: hope in God. He is the health of the countenance, the merry heart that the face shows.

note.label: Shapen in Iniquity: Resetting the Nervous System

points: Correction is grievous unto him that forsaketh the way. One of the key points in the root of bitterness is correction: people become bitter a lot of times when they are corrected. Brothers get corrected, and in their mind Satan enters and says, they hate you, they never liked you, they are not right. And you are listening to all these thoughts, which is Satan. Like Wormtongue whispering in the king's ear: it is either Satan in your mind, or the person next to you speaking evil in your ears and you listening to it.

Before bitterness becomes a root, it must be a seed first. Something gets whispered in your mind, and once that seed starts growing into roots inside of you, you change, and you change for the worse. You might think nobody sees your change; you come to class and try to play it off, but everybody sees it, because you cannot hide bitterness.

Did Cain forsake the way? Was Cain corrected? Yes. The Lord corrected him and said, if you do well I will accept you, and Cain refused the correction; it was grievous to him, he became bitter against his brother, and he went and killed him.

He that hateth reproof shall die. If you hate when you are corrected, and you do not want anybody to tell you anything, you are going to die. Some of you might get corrected harshly, and you get offended and say, I am not coming to the school anymore. Come on, man: what shall separate you from the love of God? You are going to let a brother speaking to you in a way you did not like separate you from Christ?

A lot of sisters, after they have been corrected by their husband, become bitter against their husband. I have seen sisters become bitter and leave the truth because their husband corrected them. Sisters do not want to take accountability; if they do something wrong, they do not want to say I am sorry, and everything has to be a fight. That is Satan doing a job on our sisters. Correction from your husband is part of him ruling over you, and to rule does not mean slavery or abuse: it means to provide for her, to guide her, to teach her, to correct her, all the things a man is supposed to do for a woman he loves. Adam's flaw was that he did not correct his wife; Eve was deceived, and Adam went along with it willingly.

A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance, but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken. Those of you who have been with us for years, we can see the change in your face when correction comes and you hold a grudge because Satan tells you it was not right. We see that dark cloud.

You stop dealing with certain brothers and keep to yourself, and that is when Satan really gets in your head with things that are not true about that man or that sister. Correction can be a good thing or a bad thing; use it to build yourself up.
A soft answer turneth away wrath, but grievous words stir up anger. This is the fight: when Satan talks in your ear, you answer with the word of God.
Men give orders, they do not beg. A man of God commands his house like Adam and Abraham, and sisters should not want a husband who asks permission for everything.

If the sister listens to Satan's 'he does not understand you,' bitterness takes root and shows up as disrespect. Respond, do not react. Strength is self-control, and crashing out will get you cast out.

Kill the thought in your mind before it becomes action. When you catch yourself thinking 'why am I thinking like this,' go fast and pray and ask the Lord to take the thoughts out, rather than acting and then, like Judas, asking what you have done.

The heart of him that hath understanding seeketh knowledge, but the mouth of fools feedeth on foolishness. Young men in the war room want that water, while brothers of fifty years in the same congregation never show up. Seek wisdom from leadership yourself; do not wait to be told to come to the desk. One brother from the Memphis camp asked to sit in the hot seat and be rebuked.

A brother said he did not know the fifty was going to be this hard; he was looking for a 401k and a pension. There is no retirement plan in this truth. Much is given, so much is required. When the Connecticut brothers drove two hours to Brooklyn for the Sabbath, Tuesdays, Wednesdays and the high holy days, sometimes with a homeless man in the car, nobody complained, because we were looking for the work.

A fool looks for who he can talk sports or his job with; a man seeking knowledge seeks the war room. Some brothers think they already have the wisdom and do not need leadership, and then correction comes and they move like a woman, all emotion.

Better is a dinner of herbs where love is Better is a dinner of herbs, meaning all you got is vegetables, where love is than a stalled ox than a stalled ox and hatred therewith. And hatred therewith. Because when a certain tribe sat down with the white man, and they had all plenteous food, there was hate in the heart of the so-called white man. They were planning to overcome them and break the treaties, okay? From there, let's go to Amos chapter.
